SIM has four major pillars: o Prevention o Detection o Resolution o Quality control & feedback • The primary scope here is IT & information security incidents: incidents that are limited to computers, network appliances, networks and the information therein and conveyed thereon. A real-life example is given below. This is an assessment of the CSIRT of a major commercial organisation, where green represents the actual team and yellow represents the reference, i.e. current best-practice Levels (mapped here to draft TI certification levels of April 2010) – this way dark green means above reference and yellow below reference – the “mixed” area which is light green is compliant with the reference. Open CSIRT Foundation et al. 2008-2019 SIM3 mkXVIIIc p.5 of 11 1. Organisation - O-1 : MANDATE Description: The CSIRT’s assignment as derived from upper management. 2. Constitution - O-2 : CONSTITUENCY Description: Who the CSIRT functions are aimed at – the “clients” of the CSIRT. 3. Authority - O-3 : AUTHORITY Description: What the CSIRT is allowed to do towards their constituency in order to accomplish their role. 4. Responsibility - O-4 : RESPONSIBILITY Description: What the CSIRT is expected to do towards their constituency in order to accomplish their role. 5. Service - O-5 : SERVICE DESCRIPTION Description: Describes what the CSIRT service is and how to reach it. 6. Minimum Requirement - O-6 : (intentionally left blank – not included in “scoring”) 7. Service Level - O-7 : SERVICE LEVEL DESCRIPTION Description: Describes the level of service to be expected from the CSIRT. 8. Incident Classification - O-8 : INCIDENT CLASSIFICATION Description: The availability and application of an incident classification scheme to recorded incidents. 9. Integration - O-9 : INTEGRATION IN EXISTING CSIRT SYSTEMS Description: Describes the CSIRT's level of membership of a well-established CSIRT co-operation, either directly or through an "upstream" CSIRT of which it is a customer/client. 10. Organisational Framework - O-10 : ORGANISATIONAL FRAMEWORK Description: Fits O-1 to O-9 together in a coherent framework document serving as the controlling document for the CSIRT. 11. Security Policy - O-11 : SECURITY POLICY Description: Describes the security framework within which the CSIRT operates. 3) A high level simplified chart. A simplified presentation of the above radar diagram can be desirable for management or constituency level presentations vulnerability/threat/scanning information from T-3 CONSOLIDATED E-MAIL SYSTEM Description: when all csirt mail is kept in one repository open to all csirt members we speak of a consolidated e-mail system T-4 INCIDENT TRACKING SYSTEM Description: A trouble ticket system or workflow software used by the csirt to register incidents and track their workflow clearification: rtir ait otrs trouble ticket systems in general T-5 RESILIENT PHONE Description the phone system available to the csirt is resilient when its uptime and time-to-fix service levels meet or exceed the csirts service requirements clarification: mobile phones are the easiest fallback mechanism for when a teams landlines are out of order minimum requirement: fallback mechanism for the case of phone system outages T-6 RESILIENT E-MAIL Description the e-mail system available to the csirt is resilient when its uptime and time-to-fix service levels meet or exceed the csirts service requirements t-7 RESILIENT INTERNET ACCESS Description the internet access available to the csirt is resilient when its uptime and time-to-fix service levels meet or exceed the csirts service requirements t-8 INCIDENT PREVENTION TOOLSET Description: A collection of tools aimed at preventing incidents from happening in the constituency the csirt operates or uses these tools or has access to the results generated by them clearification: ipsc virus scanning spam filters port scanning if not applicable as for a purely coordinating csirt choose -1 as level and will be omitted from “scoring” t-9 INCIDENT DETECTION TOOLSET Description: A collection of tools aimed at detecting incidents when they happen or are near happening the csirt operates or uses these tools or has access to the results generated by them clearification: ids quarantinenets netflow analysis t-10 INCIDENT RESOLUTION TOOLSET Description a collection of tools aimed at resolving incidents after they have happened the csirt operates or uses these tools or has access to the results generated by them clearification: basic csirt tools including whois traceroute etc forensic toolkits clarification: eg phishing copyright issues P-1 ESCALATION TO GOVERNANCE LEVEL Description process of escalation to upper management for csirts who are a part of the same host organisation as their constituency for external constituencies escalation to governance levels of constituents p-2 ESCALATION TO PRESS FUNCTION Description process of escalation to the csirt’s host organisation’s press

metadata.title: SIM3: Security Incident Management Maturity Model

additional_metadata.General information about Best Practices: This practice focuses on evaluating and improving the maturity of Security Incident Management (SIM) capabilities through the SIM3 model. SIM is treated as a holistic process comprising four core pillars: prevention, detection, resolution, and quality control with feedback. The main scope covers IT and information security incidents—those affecting computers, network devices, and the data transmitted or stored within them. The model, however, is adaptable and can be applied to wider or narrower scopes as appropriate. For clarity and ease of reference, the term "CSIRT" is used throughout to describe any capability—whether a team, service, or function—that is subject to SIM3 assessment, even though "ISIMC" (Information Security Incident Management Capability) is more accurate. It is also noted that "CERT", a term commonly used interchangeably with CSIRT, is a trademark owned by Carnegie Mellon University in the United States and should only be used with proper authorisation. This practice provides a structured means for organisations to benchmark and enhance their incident management maturity.
additional_metadata.Time coverage: Primarily adopted across Europe (EU27) through the TF-CSIRT / Trusted Introducer community, this practice is also highly relevant to other regional and global CSIRT networks such as APCERT, LACNIC, and AfricaCERT. It is applied internationally by national, sectoral, and corporate CERTs/CSIRTs, including those in associated and partner countries, demonstrating its broad applicability and recognition beyond the EU.
additional_metadata.Geographic coverage:
Primarily adopted in Europe (EU27) through the TF-CSIRT / Trusted Introducer community, but also relevant to APCERT, LACNIC, AfricaCERT, and other regional and global CSIRT networks.
It is used internationally by national, sectoral, and corporate CERTs/CSIRTs, including in associated countries.
additional_metadata.Primary objective: To provide a structured, standardised model for assessing and improving the maturity of Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs) across operational, human, process, and tooling domains.
additional_metadata.Secondary objective:
Enable CSIRTs to benchmark their maturity levels across 44 parameters (organised into Governance, Human, Tools, and Process groups).
Support certification and accreditation of CSIRTs through objective, repeatable evaluation criteria.
Foster trust and interoperability among national and sectoral CSIRTs through harmonised best practices.
Encourage continuous development and structured capacity-building within and between CSIRT communities.
additional_metadata.Implementation strategy:
Parameter-based self-assessment: Teams assess their current standing using the 44 SIM3 parameters, graded on a scale of maturity.
Trusted Introducer (TI) evaluations: In Europe, SIM3 is the foundation of the TI accreditation and certification framework for CSIRTs under TF-CSIRT.
Third-party assessments: Can be conducted by independent evaluators for impartiality, especially for formal recognition or audits.
Progressive development: Teams use SIM3 to identify areas for improvement and structure future development roadmaps.
Customizable adaptation: Though standard, SIM3 can be extended or tailored (e.g. SIM3 for SOCs or adapted to sectoral teams).
additional_metadata.Success factors:
Wide community adoption: Recognised by European and global CSIRT networks (e.g., TF-CSIRT, FIRST, APCERT).
Balanced design: Covers governance, process, and technical dimensions equally, ensuring holistic maturity evaluation.
Certifiable and trust-building: Forms the core of TI’s certification process, adding institutional trust across EU CSIRTs.
Simplicity and clarity: Clearly defined parameters and maturity levels make it accessible to teams at different development stages.
additional_metadata.Challenges:
Requires time and engagement: Full assessment and implementation can be resource-intensive, especially for smaller teams.
Not fully automated: It relies on qualitative judgment and interviews, limiting speed and scale of mass assessments.
Voluntary model: SIM3 is not legally mandated, so uptake may depend on network incentives or peer pressure.
Sustainability of updates: Regular updating is required to align with evolving threats and CSIRT functions (though this is managed well by Open CSIRT Foundation).
additional_metadata.Alignment with EU Policies:
NIS Directive / NIS2: SIM3 helps CSIRTs meet their NIS2 obligations regarding capabilities, coordination, and incident response readiness.
EU Cybersecurity Act: Complements certification and assurance schemes through capacity assessment and trust mechanisms.
ENISA CSIRT maturity activities: SIM3 is fully compatible with ENISA’s capability development and maturity model mappings.
Digital Europe & Horizon projects: Used in EU-funded CSIRT/SOC capacity-building programs and public-private partnerships.
additional_metadata.Transferability:
Highly transferable to:
National and sectoral CSIRTs across EU, Eastern Partnership, ASEAN, and Latin America.
Security Operations Centres (SOCs), which can adapt SIM3 methodology to their structure (see SIM3 for SOCs extension).
Non-profit and critical infrastructure CSIRTs operating in resource-constrained environments.
Reusable by donor and capacity-building programs for audits, evaluations, and training frameworks.
additional_metadata.Comment: This practice offers strategic, scalable, and ethically aligned cooperation that strengthens cyber resilience, enhances trust, and promotes unified standards between key allies. It is particularly suitable for expanding dual-use cybersecurity policy instruments at EU and transatlantic levels.
additional_metadata.Comments: A highly scalable, efficient, and ethically sound best practice that significantly improves the foundations of cyber incident response across diverse settings—especially suited for EU and global public-private cooperation.
